People ask me what a commodity lawyer does all day, and the honest answer is that she reads. My associate reads the first version, I read the difficult clauses, and the client reads the summary we write in one page. Nobody in this office goes to court in a normal month. The work happens before the problem, not after it. A colleague of mine puts it very well. She says a contract is a machine for disagreeing politely, and if you build the machine properly, nobody ever has to use it. That is why we spend so long on the words. It also explains why we charge a second fee when a dispute starts. By then the machine has failed, and the work is a different kind of work.

Here is something that surprises people about the grain trade. The cargo often changes owner three or four times while the ship is still at sea. A trader in Geneva sells it to a buyer in Cairo, that buyer sells it again before the ship arrives, and every one of those sales has a contract behind it. Nobody sees the corn. What they see is a document. So the lawyer who works in this market never asks what the product looks like. He asks who owns it today, what the contract says about a late ship, and which country decides if the two sides disagree. That last question is the one that costs money when nobody answers it in advance.
